file: papers/pdf/Vogel - 2017 - From Venture Idea to Venture Opportunity.pdf
about: A conceptual framework tracing the early venture process from triggers and paths of venture idea generation (intentional, accidental discovery, legacy) through incubation and evaluation of a venture concept to exploitation.

candidates.label: Accidental discovery path
candidates.definition: A path of venture idea generation in which the idea arises unintentionally, purely by accident, while looking for something else or not looking for anything specific.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes coming up with the venture idea by accident rather than through deliberate search for an idea.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person was actively searching for an idea (intentional idea generation) or received the idea from someone else (legacy).

candidates.label: Mishap while working on something else
candidates.definition: An unplanned event during other work, such as a forgotten dough turning to flakes or noticing an unexpected material property, sets off the venture idea.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an unplanned occurrence or accident during an unrelated task that revealed something new and led to a business idea.

candidates.label: Recognising commercial potential of accident
candidates.definition: After the accidental finding, the person has the insight that it can be combined or turned into a business, and moves to commercialise it.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes realising an accidental result could become a product or business, often after positive reactions from users.

candidates.label: Intentional idea generation
candidates.definition: The person actively searches for a venture idea because of a desire to start, a resource to commercialise, or a customer need, often using techniques like brainstorming or design thinking.
candidates.applies_when: The account shows deliberate search for an idea or market for a technology.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The idea came unintentionally while doing something else (accidental discovery).

candidates.label: Legacy: idea received from others
candidates.definition: Receiving a venture idea from someone else, either through deliberate external search (e.g., crowdsourcing) or without seeking it, as when a friend suggests opening a business.
candidates.applies_when: The account says the venture idea came from another person, whether solicited or unsolicited.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person generated the idea themselves, intentionally or by accident.

candidates.label: Triggers: resource push, market pull, desire to start
candidates.definition: Idea generation is set off by a resource to commercialise, a recognised customer segment or need, or simply the wish to be an entrepreneur; these are not mutually exclusive.
candidates.applies_when: An account identifies what started the idea search or generation: a technology/resource at hand, a noticed need, or a desire to start a business.

candidates.label: Builds on prior ideas
candidates.definition: Idea generation rarely happens in a void; venture ideas build on existing own idea sets and others' ideas and take time to form.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes the idea emerging from earlier ideas or variations they or others had.

candidates.label: Idea as starting point needing incubation
candidates.definition: An initial idea, however generated, is necessary but not sufficient; the entrepreneur must incubate it by collecting missing knowledge, shaping and refining the venture concept, and evaluating desirability and feasibility before exploitation.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes an initial insight followed by work to refine, test and evaluate it before launching.

candidates.label: Social ties in incubation
candidates.definition: Accumulating missing knowledge about the venture idea often involves the entrepreneur's social ties.
candidates.applies_when: The person uses contacts to gather information to develop the venture concept.

candidates.label: Individual and external factors shape paths
candidates.definition: Prior experience, cognitive style, external pressure and environment may modify the likelihood of different idea-generation paths, including accidental discovery.
candidates.applies_when: The account links the way the idea arose to experience, environment or pressure.

candidates.label: Retrospective bias in idea origin accounts
candidates.definition: Retrospective accounts of idea generation are prone to recall bias and post hoc rationalisation.
candidates.applies_when: An account of how the idea arose appears reconstructed or rationalised after the fact.

candidates.label: Path-breaking poorly specified opportunities
candidates.definition: Some of the most path-breaking venture opportunities came about because they could not be understood well enough to be specified during incubation.
candidates.applies_when: The person moved to exploitation with a venture they could not fully specify beforehand.
